blocks.text: Keep a summary of the loop

A counter records the number of cases; an accumulator combines a contribution from each case. Both may start at zero and still represent different quantities. If we process orders, counting orders is not the same as adding up items. Naming objects after their meaning helps prevent a calculation that works mechanically but answers the wrong question.

To add contributions, an accumulator usually starts at 0: nothing has been included yet. On every iteration, we add the new contribution to the previous total. The update total=total+aporte must preserve everything collected so far; writing total=aporte replaces the summary with the latest value.

The example collects 1, 2, 3, and 4: the successive totals are 1, 3, 6, and 10. These values belong to the accumulator; the contributions are 1, 2, 3, and 4. Mixing those two columns in a trace can make an update seem correct without revealing what each object represents.

blocks.text: The initial state matters even when there are no values

If a loop has no iterations, the accumulator keeps its initial value. A sum over no contributions should produce 0, not an uninitialized value. That starting value connects the summary's meaning to its implementation. A previous total other than 0 may be correct if it represents an initial quantity that truly belongs to the problem.

Not every summary starts at 0. When multiplying contributions, the value that leaves the first factor unchanged is 1. Initializing a product to 0 would make all products zero. For minimums and maximums, we will not choose an arbitrary starting value without justification: when we reach collections, we will first check whether any initial data exist.

blocks.text: In the lab, change the limit to 1 and then to 5. Before running, predict the number of contributions and their sum. Next, add a separate counter before the loop, increment it once per iteration, and extend the output to show the number of cases as well. Do not treat the total number of items as the number of orders.

After adding the counter, check two distinct quantities: total adds the items, while pedidos counts how many contributions were processed. Both are initialized before the loop; on each iteration, the contribution is added to one and one unit is added to the other. The summary is printed after the loop.

With a limit of 1, this version summarizes Pieces=1;Orders=1. With a limit of 5, it prints Pieces=15;Orders=5. The five contributions are 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. A correct sum paired with a counter of 15 does not meet the requirement: it confuses items with orders. You may choose other clear labels as long as you preserve and check both quantities.
